title: Sourdough Pretzels Recipe: Using a Scraper for Easy Shaping
meta_description: Learn how to make sourdough pretzels with a professional twist. Discover the secret to easy shaping using a dough scraper for perfect, salty knots.
html:
There is something uniquely satisfying about a homemade sourdough pretzel. You get that characteristic tang of a long-fermented dough combined with the deep, mahogany crust and salty punch of a traditional Bavarian pretzel. However, if you've ever tried to roll out sourdough, you know it can be sticky and stubborn.

The secret to success isn't just in the starter; it's in the tools you use. When learning how to make sourdough pretzels, the right equipment makes the difference between a sticky mess and a bakery-quality twist. For me, that game-changer was incorporating a dedicated dough scraper into my workflow.

The Ingredients You'll Need

Before we dive into the shaping, let's get your mise en place ready. You will need a mature, active sourdough starter. If your starter is sluggish, feed it 4-6 hours before you plan to mix your dough to ensure a good rise.

    n
  • Active Sourdough Starter: 1/2 cup (100g)
  • Warm Water: 1 cup (230g)
  • Bread Flour: 3 to 3.5 cups (approx. 400-450g)
  • Salt: 1.5 teaspoons
  • Baking Soda: 1/2 cup (for the boiling bath)
  • Melted Butter: For brushing after baking
  • Coarse Sea Salt: For topping

Mixing and Bulk Fermentation

Start by whisking your starter and warm water together until the starter is mostly dissolved. I highly recommend using a Danish dough whisk here; its open loop design cuts through the thick starter and flour without overworking the dough or leaving clumps of dry flour at the bottom of the bowl.

Stir in your flour and salt until a shaggy dough forms. Cover the bowl with a damp cloth and let it undergo bulk fermentation. Depending on the temperature of your kitchen, this usually takes 6 to 10 hours. You are looking for the dough to double in size and feel airy to the touch. Once it's ready, gently degas the dough and move to the shaping phase.

How to Make Sourdough Pretzels: The Shaping Secret

This is where most home bakers struggle. Sourdough is more elastic than commercial yeast dough, which can make it spring back when you try to roll it. To get those clean, uniform logs, you need a tool that handles the dough without sticking to your hands.

I use the 3-in-1 Sourdough Whisk Set (Whisk, Scraper, Lame) for this entire process. Specifically, the dough scraper is essential for dividing the dough into equal portions. Instead of using a knife—which can tear the gluten structure—the scraper allows you to cleanly slice the dough into 8-10 equal pieces.

Once divided, use the scraper to help you tuck the edges of the dough under themselves, creating a smooth surface. Then, roll the piece into a long rope. If the dough sticks to your counter, use the scraper to lift and move the rope easily. To form the pretzel, make a long cylinder, form a "U" shape, cross the ends twice, and press them into the bottom of the "U".

The Alkaline Bath and Baking

The deep brown color and distinct pretzel flavor come from a process called the Maillard reaction, which is accelerated by an alkaline environment. Bring a large pot of water to a near-boil and stir in the baking soda.

Carefully drop each shaped pretzel into the water for about 30 seconds. Do not over-boil them, or they will lose their ability to expand in the oven. Use a slotted spoon to move them onto a parchment-lined baking sheet. Immediately sprinkle with coarse sea salt.

Bake at 425°F (220°C) for 12-15 minutes. If you want a more professional look, you can use the bread scoring lame from the 3-in-1 Sourdough Whisk Set to make a quick shallow slash across the top of the pretzel before boiling; this allows for a beautiful, controlled burst during the bake.

Pro Tips for the Perfect Crust

For that glossy, golden finish, brush the pretzels with melted butter the second they come out of the oven. The heat from the pretzel will soak the butter deep into the crust. If you prefer a more traditional German style, you can brush them with a diluted lye solution instead of baking soda, though baking soda is safer and more accessible for most home kitchens.

If you find your dough is too sticky to handle, resist the urge to dump in handfuls of extra flour. Instead, rely on your dough scraper to move and shape the dough. Too much extra flour can lead to a dense, dry pretzel that lacks that signature chew.

FAQ

Can I freeze sourdough pretzel dough?

Yes. After the bulk fermentation, shape your pretzels and place them on a tray in the freezer. Once frozen solid, transfer them to a freezer bag. Thaw them in the fridge overnight before boiling and baking.

Why aren't my pretzels browning?

This is usually due to the boiling bath. Ensure your water is hot and you have used enough baking soda. If the water isn't alkaline enough, you won't get that deep mahogany color.

My pretzels are too flat. What went wrong?

Over-proofing is the most common cause. If the dough ferments too long, the gluten structure weakens and the pretzels flatten out during the boil. Stick to the doubling-in-size rule rather than a specific time limit.
